lesson.title: Limit Existence: Turning the Left-Right Match Into a Rule
lesson.summary: The left-right comparison becomes a general theorem for limit existence, and separating the three distinct ways a limit can fail to exist, disagreement, unbounded growth, and oscillation, turns graph-reading guesswork into a reliable algebraic check.
lesson.body:
The comparisons made in the last section, checking whether the left-hand and right-hand limits agree, are not just a computational trick for one or two examples; they form a general theorem that governs whether any limit exists at all. The existence rule states: lim(x to a) f(x) exists if and only if both one-sided limits lim(x to a-) f(x) and lim(x to a+) f(x) exist and are equal to each other. When that condition holds, the common value of the two one-sided limits is the value of the two-sided limit. When it fails, for any reason, the two-sided limit simply does not exist, full stop; there is no fallback value to report.

There are three distinct ways a limit can fail to exist, and it is worth separating them clearly. First, the one-sided limits can both exist but disagree, as with the floor function at x = 2, where the left side settled on 1 and the right side settled on 2. Second, one or both one-sided limits can fail to settle on any finite number at all, growing without bound instead, as happens with f(x) = 1/x^2 near x = 0, where both sides increase without bound rather than approaching a single number. Third, a function can oscillate infinitely often near the target with no settling behavior at all, as with f(x) = sin(1/x) near x = 0, which sweeps repeatedly between -1 and 1 no matter how close x gets to 0, never approaching one fixed value.

Let's apply the existence rule to a case built to succeed, a piecewise function: f(x) = x + 1 for x < 1, and f(x) = x^2 + 1 for x >= 1. Compute the left-hand limit as x approaches 1 from below, using the first piece, since that piece governs inputs below 1: as x to 1-, x + 1 approaches 2. Compute the right-hand limit as x approaches 1 from above, using the second piece (which also governs x = 1 itself, though that value is not needed for the limit): as x to 1+, x^2 + 1 approaches 1^2 + 1 = 2. Both one-sided limits equal 2, so by the existence rule, lim(x to 1) f(x) exists and equals 2, even though the function is defined by two completely different formulas on either side of x = 1.

Notice that this piecewise function's limit exists precisely because the two formula pieces meet up smoothly at x = 1, both landing on output 2; a small change to either piece, say using x^2 + 2 instead, would break the match and cause the two-sided limit to fail to exist, even though each one-sided limit individually would still exist just fine.

These three failure patterns, disagreement between sides, unbounded growth, and endless oscillation, will each get more formal treatment in later chapters, including precise notation for infinite limits, but recognizing them here by their behavior is already enough to correctly answer "does this limit exist" without needing that extra machinery yet.

This existence rule is what makes the left-hand and right-hand limit machinery worth building in the first place: rather than staring at a graph and guessing whether it "looks continuous" at a point, you now have a two-step algebraic check, compute each side, compare the results, that settles the question with certainty every time.
